topics.name: Order of operations
topics.plain: The agreed order for the steps in a line of arithmetic: brackets first, then powers, then multiplying and dividing, then adding and taking away.
topics.size: Only sections of two pages teach it (first-steps and numbers-a-computer-can-hold), so it is small, and it comes at the very start. Polynomials need it, because working out a many-term expression is where the order first matters; the Zen letters and balance pages keep to one operation or a picture, so letters for numbers does not. The closer look on v - u / a stays with rearranging formulas, the page it follows.

topics.name: The number line and negative numbers
topics.plain: One long line holds whole numbers, fractions and negative numbers in order, and further right is bigger. Moving right adds and moving left takes away. A number below zero is negative.
topics.size: One page (about 1,550 words). Coordinates and the families of numbers both need it, so it is a topic. The Zen module puts it with graphs; it sits here because a learner looks for negative numbers under number.

topics.name: Families of numbers
topics.plain: Numbers come in families, each inside the next: the counting numbers, the integers, the fractions (rational numbers) and every point on the line (real numbers). Each new family answers a question the one before could not, like 3 − 5 or 7 ÷ 2.
topics.size: Sections of three pages, about one sitting in any course. The old list made seven topics here, one for each family. Every page teaches them together, as one table, and nothing needs one family without the others, so one topic. No page teaches computable numbers, and the complex numbers are taught by the algebra area's pages.

topics.name: What a fraction is
topics.plain: A fraction is some of the equal slices of one whole. The bottom number says how many slices the whole is cut into. The top number says how many of them you have.
topics.size: One short page (about 1,050 words), the first mathematics in The Zen of Slashes and Surds. A beginner arriving here needs a small step, and every other fraction topic, the dividing rule for powers and the number line all need it.

topics.name: Equivalent fractions
topics.plain: Different fractions can be the same amount, like one half and two quarters. Multiplying or dividing the top and the bottom by the same number keeps the amount the same. Dividing them makes the fraction simpler.
topics.size: One short page (about 1,030 words). Comparing and adding both need it on its own, so it is a topic and not a step inside either.

topics.name: Multiplying fractions
topics.plain: A fraction of a fraction, like half of a half. Multiply the tops, then multiply the bottoms. Multiplying by a fraction smaller than 1 makes a number smaller.
topics.size: One page (about 1,580 words) and a short closer look on the idea that multiplying always makes a number bigger. Dividing needs it, and adding does not, so it stands apart from adding.

topics.name: Comparing fractions
topics.plain: Finding which of two fractions is bigger. You can look at the size of the slices, count the slices, see where each one sits between 0, one half and 1, or give both the same bottom number.
topics.size: One page (about 1,370 words). Nothing later needs it, but it is a skill a learner names and a short check can confirm, and near the start one page is a whole topic. It could become a step in equivalent fractions if the map wants fewer towns here.

topics.name: Adding and subtracting fractions
topics.plain: Putting fractions together and taking one away from another. When the slices are the same size, you count them. When they are not, you first cut both into slices of one size.
topics.size: Two short pages, about 2,550 words, so under two sittings. Nothing later needs taking away without adding, and they are always taught together, so one topic.

topics.name: Dividing fractions
topics.plain: Dividing asks how many of one thing fit into another. To divide by a fraction, turn it over and multiply. A fraction and its turned-over partner make 1.
topics.size: One page (about 1,160 words). Fractions with letters need the partner idea from here on its own, so it is a topic, not a step in multiplying.

topics.name: Fractions with letters in them
topics.plain: The same moves with fractions when a shape or a letter stands for a number. Give two fractions the same bottom before you add them, cancel what is on the top and the bottom, and use a fraction's turned-over partner.
topics.size: One Zen page (about 1,110 words) or one Dewey Track section: under a sitting on either route, after the fraction topics, which the learner now carries as single moves. The number and algebra searches both proposed it, as the same idea. It sits at the end of the fractions district because everything it needs is there: the Zen page puts shapes in the fractions itself, so it does not need 'Letters for numbers', and nothing in algebra needs it.

topics.name: What a power is
topics.plain: A power is a number multiplied by itself again and again. The small raised number says how many times: 2 to the power 3 is 2 × 2 × 2, which is 8.
topics.size: The Zen page is short (about 900 words), and the Dewey Track and the integrated course each teach it in one section (the integrated section opens 'A power is a short way to write repeated multiplication' and then gives every rule), so about one sitting. Every power rule, roots, logarithms and binary need it.

topics.name: Multiplying powers
topics.plain: When you multiply two powers of the same number, you add the small raised numbers: 2³ × 2⁴ = 2⁷. Write both the long way and count, and you can see why.
topics.size: One Zen page (about 1,170 words), plus one section each on the Dewey Track and in the integrated course. It is split from dividing because the rule for the logarithm of a product, multiplying in scientific notation and halfway powers need the adding rule without the subtracting one.

topics.name: Dividing powers and the zero power
topics.plain: When you divide two powers of the same number, you take away the small raised numbers, because pairs on the top and the bottom cancel. When everything cancels, the answer is 1, so any number to the power 0 is 1.
topics.size: Two short pages, about 2,100 words. The zero power is a step here, not a topic: nothing needs it on its own, and it is the dividing rule when everything cancels. It needs the pizza page's idea that a number over itself is 1.

topics.name: Negative powers
topics.plain: A negative power means one over the power: 2 to the power −3 is 1/8. It comes from dividing when the bottom has more. The minus sign does not make the number negative.
topics.size: One page (about 1,600 words). Scientific notation for small numbers needs it on its own, so it is a topic and not a step in dividing.

topics.name: A power of a power
topics.plain: A power raised to another power: (2²)³ means three boxes of 2 × 2. Multiply the small raised numbers, so (2²)³ = 2⁶.
topics.size: One short page (about 1,070 words). Fractional powers need it without negative powers, so it stands apart from them, and from multiplying, which other topics need without it.

topics.name: Scientific notation
topics.plain: A short way to write very big and very small numbers: a number from 1 to 10 times a power of ten, like 2.59 × 10¹⁰. Python writes the same number as 2.59e10.
topics.size: One page (about 1,790 words), the view from the top of the powers strand, but it names and teaches a new idea, so it is a topic. Small numbers need negative powers and multiplying them needs the adding rule. Log scales need it.

topics.name: Square roots and cube roots
topics.plain: A square root undoes a square: it is the side of a square with that area. The square root of 49 is 7, because 7 × 7 = 49. A cube root undoes a cube in the same way.
topics.size: One Zen page (about 1,570 words), or one section of Machines that take a number on the Dewey Track, which defines the square root, math.sqrt and why the square root of -4 fails. Surds, fractional powers, spread and distance all need it, and it needs only what a power is.

topics.name: Logarithms: how many times you multiply
topics.plain: A logarithm answers the question "how many times did we multiply?". The logarithm base 10 of 1000 is 3, because three steps of ×10 go from 1 to 1000. It also tells you about how many digits a number has.
topics.size: One Zen page (about 1,160 words) and one section in each of the other two courses. It needs only what a power is, not the power rules, so it can come early. Binary search's speed is where the Dewey Track puts it to work.

topics.name: Surds: roots with endless decimals
topics.plain: Most square roots, like the square root of 2, are not whole numbers or fractions, and their decimals never end. A root left written as a root is called a surd. Some surds can be made simpler.
topics.size: One page (about 1,580 words). It is where the idea of a number that is not a fraction first becomes real, so it is its own topic and not a step in square roots.

topics.name: Rules of logarithms
topics.plain: When numbers multiply, their logarithms add: log(a × b) = log a + log b. A slide rule multiplies two numbers by adding two lengths, using this rule.
topics.size: One Zen page (about 1,550 words) and a section each elsewhere. Split from logarithms because log scales and counting digits need logarithms without these rules.

topics.name: Doubling and exponential growth
topics.plain: Something that doubles, or grows by the same factor at every step, grows much faster than people expect. A logarithm tells you how many steps it takes to reach a size. Halving works the same way, backwards.
topics.size: One long Dewey Track page (about 3,340 words, shared with the two rule topics for one section), a little over two sittings. It needs binary search as well as logarithms: the page sits after Finding things fast in 'Algorithms that scale', its warm-up and its last section run binary search again, and it counts with while and for loops throughout. That puts it deep enough that a learner carries powers and logarithms as chunks. Doubling and halving stay one topic, because the page teaches them as one idea: the two questions have the same answer.

topics.name: Fractional powers
topics.plain: A power can be a fraction. Two half powers make one whole power, so 9 to the power one half is the square root of 9. In 8 to the power two thirds, the bottom of the fraction takes a root and the top takes a power.
topics.size: Two pages, about 3,000 words, near the top of what a learner here meets, and the learner carries the power rules as chunks by now. Nothing needs the half power without the top and bottom of the fraction, so the two pages are one topic.

topics.name: Log scales: each step multiplies
topics.plain: On a log scale, equal gaps mean equal multiplying, not equal adding. One picture can then show things that differ by millions, from a virus to the planets.
topics.size: One page (about 1,900 words), the view from the top of the Zen graphs strand, but it teaches a new idea (the logarithmic scale), so it is a topic. Its Kepler section uses fractional powers as a stretch, not a need.

topics.name: Place value and binary
topics.plain: Each column of a number is worth a power of the base: ones, tens and hundreds in base 10. Binary is base 2. It uses only 0 and 1, and its columns are worth 1, 2, 4, 8 and so on. This is how a computer counts.
topics.size: About a sitting and a half on the Dewey Track (the first half of Everything is ones and zeros, listed whole: its hexadecimal and float sections are other topics' steps, and one section of Numbers a computer can hold); one section of How programming languages came to be on the integrated course. Split from hexadecimal because XOR and parity, and floats, need binary without hex. The page writes binary columns as powers of 2, so it needs what a power is (the pair decision MIT-1.1 before MIT-1.4).

topics.name: Hexadecimal: binary written short
topics.plain: Base 16, with the digits 0 to 9 and then A to F. One hex digit is exactly four bits, so hex is a short way to write binary. A screen colour like #FF8800 is three bytes written in hex.
topics.size: The second half of one Dewey page, about one sitting, or one section of How programming languages came to be. XOR and parity, and floats, need binary without hex, so hex is a topic of its own. The CSS colour pages use hex colours but explain the pairs themselves, so they do not need it. No page teaches arithmetic in hex, which MIT-1.4 names.

topics.name: Why 0.1 + 0.2 is not 0.3
topics.plain: A computer keeps a decimal as the nearest binary fraction it can hold, in about 16 digits. So 0.1 + 0.2 gives 0.30000000000000004. Compare such numbers as "close enough", not "exactly equal".
topics.size: One section and one context page (about 1,670 words). The context page teaches an idea other topics need (testing a function that returns a float, numerical methods, every float surprise on the site), so it is the main teaching page of a topic of its own rather than a context step.

topics.name: Bits that flip: XOR and parity
topics.plain: XOR gives 1 when two bits are different. Used on whole numbers, it flips chosen bits. A parity bit records whether a message has an odd or even number of 1s, so one flipped bit can be caught.
topics.size: One long page (about 2,530 words) that joins logic to bits. It teaches bitwise XOR, masks and parity, which the truth-table pages do not, so it is a topic and not a step there.

topics.name: Truth tables
topics.plain: A table of what a rule gives for every possible input of true and false. It defines and, or, not and exclusive or (XOR). With n inputs there are 2ⁿ rows.
topics.size: One long Dewey page (about 2,790 words) or two sections of the integrated course's logic page. It needs conditions in an if statement first, as the pair decision PDP-LO6 before MIT-2.4 says: learners meet true and false there, and the table names what they already do.

topics.name: De Morgan's laws
topics.plain: Two rules for turning a "not" inside out. Not (A and B) is the same as (not A) or (not B), and not (A or B) is (not A) and (not B). They make a tangled condition easy to read, and they work on sets too.
topics.size: One long Dewey page (about 2,760 words) or the second half of the integrated course's logic page. It needs truth tables to check each law in every case. The section on sets uses set operations, but the laws themselves do not need them.

topics.name: Sets and set operations
topics.plain: A set is a collection with no order and no repeats. You can ask whether something is in it, and combine two sets: everything in either (union), everything in both (intersection), or everything in one but not the other (difference).
topics.size: Each course teaches it on one page (3,190 words on the Dewey Track, 1,680 in the integrated course), so a learner meets one to two sittings; the word count here adds two parallel pages. Set language and the operations are always taught together and nothing needs one without the other, so one topic. The complement, the Cartesian product and the power set are steps. Both pages build sets in Python from lists.

topics.name: Venn diagrams
topics.plain: Drawing sets as overlapping circles inside a box, so each region can be pointed at. With two or three circles you can count what is in either, in both, or in exactly two, without counting anything twice.
topics.size: Two parallel pages (3,480 words on the Dewey Track, 1,350 in the integrated course), so one to two and a half sittings for a learner. Counting with overlaps (inclusion-exclusion) is taught on the picture on both pages, so it is a step, not a topic; probability's "or" rule in the chance area uses it.

topics.name: Letters for numbers
topics.plain: A box, a shape or a letter can stand for a number. An expression like 3x + 2 has a value once you choose a number for x. An equation says two sides are equal, like x + 3 = 7, and solving it means finding the number that makes it true.
topics.size: Three routes into one idea: a whole Zen page for a beginner (about 1,370 words), the slot section of Machines that take a number and two sections of Rules with letters in them on the Dewey Track, or one integrated-course section; about one sitting on any route. The number search called the Zen page 'Unknowns' and the algebra search called the others 'Expressions and equations'; both teach that a letter stands for a number and that an equation says two sides are equal, and every later topic needs the two together, so they merge. It needs nothing: the Zen page keeps to one operation at a time, and the balance page shows 2 × □ + 1 as boxes and beads, so the order of operations waits for polynomials, where a many-term expression is first worked out. The slot section (unit 4) is the Dewey Track's first step here, so Dewey learners meet letters before Running a formula backwards.

topics.name: Polynomials and like terms
topics.plain: A polynomial is a sum of terms such as 3x² and 5x. The number in front of each term is its coefficient, and the highest power is its degree. Collecting like terms adds the terms with the same power, so the expression gets shorter and keeps its value.
topics.size: About one sitting on either course (DT's terms, evaluate tool and like terms; PMI's five polynomial sections). Collecting like terms is adding two polynomials in both courses, so they are one topic. Linear equations and graphs need this without expanding brackets. It needs lists because both teaching pages keep a polynomial as a Python list from their first cell (collecting like terms is adding two lists place by place), and the order of operations because working out a many-term expression such as 2 + 15t - 4.9t² is the first place the order matters. So the algebra from here on is on the Python routes; see the question.

topics.name: Expanding brackets
topics.plain: Multiplying every term in one bracket by every term in the other, then collecting like terms. Two brackets make a quadratic, and three make a cubic. (a + b)² is not a² + b².
topics.size: One long section in DT, three in PMI: about one sitting. Old MIT-1.6's expanding half and MIT-1.8 are taught as one move in both courses, so they merge. Factorising and completing the square need it.

topics.name: Doing the same to both sides
topics.plain: An equation is like a balance. Any move is allowed, as long as you do the same move to both sides, so the two sides stay equal. To get a letter on its own, undo the steps in the opposite order.
topics.size: A whole Zen page for a beginner, or the opening section of the rearranging page in the Dewey Track and the integrated course: about one sitting. The number and algebra searches both built a topic on keeping-it-level; they are one idea. Solving linear equations, rearranging and inequalities each need it without the others, so it is its own topic.

topics.name: Solving linear equations
topics.plain: Finding the one value of x that makes an equation like 5x − 4 = 2x + 11 true, one move at a time, and checking it by putting it back into both sides. Any linear equation can be tidied into ax + b = 0, so x = −b/a.
topics.size: Two DT sections, one PMI section: under a sitting. No descriptor names it and the old list had no topic for it, but both courses teach it and simultaneous equations need it.

topics.name: Rearranging formulas
topics.plain: Changing a formula so that it finds a different letter. Speed, distance and time are one formula written three ways. Some cases need care: the letter behind a minus sign, the letter twice, the letter on the bottom, and a square that has two roots.
topics.size: Most of one page in each course, about one and a half sittings. The harder cases (letter twice, letter underneath) are not needed separately by anything later, so they stay steps.

topics.name: Solving inequalities
topics.plain: Solving for a range of values, not one value: not 'x is 5' but 'x is anything above 5'. The moves are the same as for an equation, except one: multiplying or dividing both sides by a negative number flips the sign, so < becomes >.
topics.size: Three sections of a DT programming page (choosing-a-path, placed by the programming area) and one PMI section: under a sitting. The Dewey Track teaches inequalities only there.

topics.name: Simultaneous equations
topics.plain: Two or three facts that must be true at the same time, and the values that make all of them true. With two unknowns, the answer is where two lines cross. Parallel lines never cross, so some systems have no single answer.
topics.size: A whole DT page and a long PMI section: one to two sittings, two and three unknowns together. The matrix method is a separate topic because it needs matrices.

topics.name: Factorising quadratics
topics.plain: Finding the two brackets that multiply to make a quadratic: expanding, run backwards. If two numbers multiply to make 0, one of them is 0, and that gives the solutions.
topics.size: Two short DT sections, one PMI section: well under a sitting in words, but factorising by inspection is slow to learn. PMI teaches the formula first and DT teaches it second, and complex numbers need the formula without factorising, so the two stay apart.

topics.name: The quadratic formula
topics.plain: A formula that solves any quadratic equation. You put in its three numbers, a, b and c. The part under the square root, the discriminant, says whether there are two solutions, one, or none on the number line.
topics.size: Three DT sections, one PMI section: about one sitting. The discriminant is read against the picture of a parabola crossing the axis, which is why graphs come first.

topics.name: Completing the square: where curves turn
topics.plain: Rewriting a quadratic as a(x − h)² + k, so that the highest or lowest point of its curve is at (h, k). Every quadratic is the same curve, moved and stretched. The same form also gives the solutions.
topics.size: One page per course, one to two sittings. Moving and stretching a graph is taught inside this topic and graphs of functions, never on its own.

topics.name: Complex numbers
topics.plain: When the quadratic formula needs the square root of a negative number, the answers still exist. They are complex numbers, such as 3 + 2i, where i × i = −1. They sit on a plane, not on a line, and multiplying by i turns a point a quarter turn.
topics.size: One page per course, about one and a half sittings. These are the only pages that teach the complex numbers, so this also succeeds the number family MIT-2.1g.

topics.name: Maths functions: one in, one out
topics.plain: A function is a machine: put a number in, and exactly one number comes out. We write f(x) for the number f gives when x goes in. Its domain is the set of numbers it accepts, and its range is the set of numbers it can give.
topics.size: Two DT sections, one PMI section: under a sitting. Graphs, inverses and composition each need it, and none needs the others. It needs writing functions in Python, not letters: both routes build the maths function from a Python one (Machines that take a number puts f(x) = 100x - 50 beside def sensor_celsius, and Functions and their graphs opens from def double), and the Dewey Track reaches its letters page three units later. The slot section is also the Dewey Track's first step in 'Letters for numbers'.

topics.name: Inverse functions
topics.plain: The inverse of a function undoes it: going there and back gives the number you started with. Not every function has one. Squaring turns 3 and −3 into 9, so no machine can tell which one went in.
topics.size: Two DT sections and one PMI section: about half a sitting to a sitting. Split from the function itself because the inverse sine, cosine and tangent (and the logarithm, in the number area) need it.

topics.name: Joining functions in a row
topics.plain: Sending the output of one function straight into another. 'g after f' is written g(f(x)). The order matters: the same two machines in the other order usually do a different job, and a function joined to its inverse changes nothing.
topics.size: One DT section, about two-thirds of a sitting. No descriptor names it, and nothing needs it: the chain rule pages build a function inside a function on the spot. It stays a town because 'g after f' is a skill a learner names and a short check confirms, and the Dewey chain rule reuses its compose().

topics.name: Graphs of functions
topics.plain: Drawing a function as a picture, with a point for every input. Lines, parabolas and cubics each have their own shape. Where the graph crosses the x-axis, the function is zero, and where two graphs cross, the two functions are equal.
topics.size: One page (DT) or most of one (PMI), about two sittings: linear, quadratic and cubic graphs and solving from a graph. It also carries gaps in a graph (1/x) and which curve grows faster (x² against 2^x).

topics.name: Coordinates
topics.plain: Two number lines at right angles make a grid. Two numbers, first across and then up, give one place on it, like the point (3, 2). Negative numbers reach below and to the left.
topics.size: One Zen page (about 1,380 words), or the first section of Drawing a rule on the Dewey Track, which defines a point's coordinates, the two axes and the origin. Every graph on the site needs it; the matrix pages use coordinates only in passing, so this is the site's one coordinates topic, at the start of Grids and straight lines.

topics.name: Patterns as graphs: lines and curves
topics.plain: You draw a list of numbers as dots on a grid. A pattern that adds the same amount at each step makes a straight line, and a pattern that multiplies makes a curve that gets steeper and steeper. A list of numbers made by a rule like this is called a sequence.
topics.size: One page (about 1,560 words). It is the first time adding and multiplying patterns (arithmetic and geometric sequences) are seen side by side, which the old list never named. Graphs of functions in the algebra area may need it.

topics.name: Slope of a line
topics.plain: How steep a line is: how far it goes up for each step across. You can find it from any two points on the line. A slope is also a rate: how much y changes when x goes up by one. A vertical line has no slope.
topics.size: The first half of a page in each course, about one sitting. Split from the equation of a line because the derivative and the tangent on the unit circle need slope and nothing else from lines.

topics.name: Equations of straight lines
topics.plain: Writing a straight line as an equation, y = mx + c or ax + by + c = 0, so that 'is this point on the line?' becomes a sum. Parallel lines have the same slope. The slopes of perpendicular lines multiply to −1.
topics.size: The second half of a page in each course, about one sitting. Parallel and perpendicular sit here because DT teaches them with line equations and nothing needs them on their own.

topics.name: Limits: what a function gets close to
topics.plain: What a function gets closer and closer to, which is not always what it does when it arrives. A limit exists only when both sides agree. A function can also settle towards a value as x grows without end.
topics.size: One page per course, about one and a half sittings. The number e and the limits of floating-point numbers are steps inside it.

topics.name: The derivative: how fast right now
topics.plain: How fast something is changing right now, not on average. Shrink the straight line between two points on a curve (a chord), and its slope settles on the slope of the curve at one point: the slope of the tangent line. Where a curve turns, the derivative is zero.
topics.size: One page per course, one to two sittings. Finding turning points with the derivative is a step here (and in the rules topic); it is too small to stand alone.

topics.name: Rules for derivatives
topics.plain: Short rules find a derivative without a limit every time: the power rule, and rules for adding, multiplying and dividing functions, and for one function inside another (the chain rule). A last section runs a rule backwards, as a first look at integration.
topics.size: One page per course, one to two sittings. Not split into the simple rules and the chain rule: deep in, the learner carries the derivative as one idea, and each half would be well under a sitting. Integration appears only as a 'going further' step. It does not need 'Joining functions in a row': only the chain rule uses it, the power, sum and product rules come first on both pages, and the integrated page builds the inner and the outer function on the spot.

topics.name: Solving an equation by computing
topics.plain: Finding where a curve crosses zero with a program instead of algebra: squeeze the answer between two guesses and halve the gap again and again, or follow the tangent line towards zero (Newton's method).
topics.size: One long page in the Dewey Track's Change unit, about two sittings. The old list had no topic for it. Bisection is binary search on a number line; Newton's method needs the derivative. It sits in Calculus, beside the derivative it follows on the Dewey Track, where a learner looking for Newton's method would look.

topics.name: The slope of a wave
topics.plain: How fast a wave is changing at each moment. The slope of sine is cosine, so a wave changes fastest where it crosses its middle line and not at all at its top.
topics.size: One PMI page, about one sitting. The old list had no topic for it; the page joins waves and derivatives, and needs the chain rule for a general wave.

topics.name: Area and perimeter
topics.plain: How far it is round the edge of a flat shape, and how much surface it covers. A rectangle's area is length times width, and a triangle is half a rectangle.
topics.size: Four short DT sections, under a sitting, plus PMI's table of formulas. Split from circles because the determinant (the area of a shape after a matrix moves it) needs area and not pi.

topics.name: Circles and pi
topics.plain: The distance round a circle, its circumference, and the surface inside it. Both use the number pi, about 3.14: the circumference is 2πr and the area is πr².
topics.size: One DT section and its tool, about half a sitting, or the integrated course's table of formulas, which gives the area and circumference of a circle and a circle_area function: small, near the start. Radians (a walk round the circle) and every round solid need circles without needing anything else here.

topics.name: Volume and surface area
topics.plain: How much a solid holds, and how much surface covers the outside: cuboids, cylinders, cones and spheres. Double every length, and the area grows four times and the volume eight times.
topics.size: The second half of the DT page (about one sitting) and PMI's formulas, with 'what doubling does' as the step on scaling.

topics.name: Pythagoras and distance
topics.plain: In a right-angled triangle, the two short sides squared add up to the long side squared. The gap across and the gap up between two points are two short sides, so this gives the distance between them. The midpoint is the point halfway.
topics.size: One page per course, one to two sittings. The old list split Pythagoras from distance, but both courses teach them as one move, and everything later that needs Pythagoras (the unit circle, triangles) needs points on a grid as well.

topics.name: Sine, cosine and the unit circle
topics.plain: Walk a point round a circle of radius 1. How far across it is and how far up it is are the cosine and sine of the angle you turned, and cos²θ + sin²θ = 1. The tangent is the slope, up over across. Angles can be in degrees or in radians, and Python uses radians.
topics.size: One page per course, about two sittings. Five old topics merge: every later topic needs sine and cosine and radians together (Python takes radians), and nothing needs the identity, the tangent or the exact values on their own. Exact values and 'triangles on a ball' are steps.

topics.name: Sine and cosine waves
topics.plain: Draw how high the point on the circle is against time, and you get a wave. Four numbers change it: how tall it is (amplitude), how often it repeats (period or frequency), where it starts (phase), and where its middle line is.
topics.size: One page per course, about one and a half sittings. The graph of the tangent, octaves and adding two waves are steps inside it.

topics.name: Right-angled triangle trigonometry
topics.plain: Given one angle and one side of a right-angled triangle, finding the other sides with sine, cosine or tangent (SOH-CAH-TOA). Going backwards, the inverse functions find an angle from two sides. This is how you measure a height you cannot reach, or a bearing.
topics.size: The first half of a page in each course, about one sitting. Finding an angle is not split off, because everything that needs the ratios also needs to find angles. Needs rearranging because a side on the bottom of a ratio (hyp = opp / sin θ) is found by changing the subject.

topics.name: The sine rule and cosine rule
topics.plain: Rules for a triangle with no right angle. The cosine rule is Pythagoras with a correction, the sine rule pairs each side with the angle opposite it, and the area is half of two sides times the sine of the angle between them. The sine rule can give two triangles that both fit.
topics.size: The second half of a page in each course, one sitting (DT) to two (PMI). Four old topics merge: both courses teach area, cosine rule, sine rule and the two-answer case together, and nothing later needs one without the others.

topics.name: Matrices that move pictures
topics.plain: A grid of numbers treated as one thing. You can add and scale grids and turn them corner to corner. A small matrix moves every point of a picture, and multiplying two matrices joins two moves into one, where the order matters.
topics.size: Three short Computational Methods pages, about two sittings together. The brief's own example: deep in, 'Matrices' is one topic. Nothing later needs the grid operations without the moves and the product.

topics.name: Undoing a matrix and solving equations
topics.plain: The determinant is one number that says how much a matrix stretches areas, and whether its move can be undone. The inverse matrix undoes it. Then several equations with several unknowns become one matrix, solved one row at a time, and NumPy does each of these jobs in one line.
topics.size: Three short pages, about two and a half sittings: the determinant and the inverse, solving a system one row at a time (solving starts from 'undo A', so the two are one idea), and Matrices in NumPy, which closes the series by doing every matrix job in one line. NumPy is a step, not a topic: it is a new tool for ideas the learner already has, nothing needs it, and the graphics pages use it only in optional 'the same in NumPy' answer boxes. It does not need area and perimeter: Undoing it measures the F with its own function and counts the squares it covers.

topics.name: Perspective: 3D on a flat screen
topics.plain: Every point in a 3D scene becomes a point on a flat screen when you divide its across and up by its depth, so far things come out small. To move the camera, subtract its position first. A point behind the camera cannot be drawn.
topics.size: Two pages, about two and a half sittings. The camera page only extends the divide, and the cube page needs both, so they are one topic. Similar triangles are a step inside it. Both pages are Computational Methods Python pages: the first cell defines project() and runs one loop inside another, and the orbit page has seven functions and an animation, so it needs writing functions and for loops, not only coordinates. The one list comprehension is in the first page's 'Your world' section, so comprehensions are not a need.

topics.name: Turning shapes in 3D
topics.plain: A matrix made from sine and cosine turns every corner of a shape about one axis. Two turns, one after the other, are one matrix: the product of the two.
topics.size: One page, about one and a half sittings.

topics.name: The camera as one matrix
topics.plain: No 3 × 3 matrix can slide a shape. Add a fourth number to every point, and sliding, turning and the camera's divide by depth all become 4 × 4 matrices, so a whole camera is one matrix.
topics.size: One page, about one and a half sittings.

topics.name: Listing and counting outcomes
topics.plain: You list every way something can end, missing none and counting none twice. Then you count them without listing them: if one choice has 3 options and the next has 4, together they have 3 × 4 = 12.
topics.size: One Dewey page (about 1.8 sittings), or two short sections of the integrated counting page. Both routes teach the list and the multiplication together, and probability by counting uses both (6 x 6 = 36 outcomes), so nothing needs the list without the principle. Merged for that reason, and because listing on its own is closer to an activity than an idea.

topics.name: Orders and choices
topics.plain: You count the ways to put things in order, to fill the first few places, and to choose a group when the order does not matter. These counts are called factorials, permutations and combinations.
topics.size: One page on each route: about 2 sittings on the Dewey Track, 1 on the integrated course. The factorial exists here to build permutations, and combinations are permutations divided down; both routes teach all three on one page, and nothing outside needs the factorial on its own, so one topic.

topics.name: Probability by counting
topics.plain: A probability says how likely something is, as a number from 0 (it cannot happen) to 1 (it is certain). When every outcome is equally likely, you count the outcomes you want and divide by all of them.
topics.size: Two sections on each route, under one sitting, which suits its place near the start. The 0-to-1 scale is a step, not a topic: the integrated page teaches the scale and equal likelihood in one section, and nothing uses the scale without counting cases. The integrated page's opening simulation is the hook for the counting, so it sits here.

topics.name: Finding a chance by simulation
topics.plain: You let the computer repeat a chance experiment many times, and count how often something happens. The share gets closer to the true chance as the runs grow, but slowly, and a few runs can be far from it.
topics.size: Four sections of How likely is it?, one of the integrated probability page, and a closer look: about one sitting. Relative frequency and the law of large numbers had no topic of their own. Kept apart from the Monte Carlo topic because the Computational Methods route reaches Monte Carlo without it, and Monte Carlo adds areas, an error that shrinks like 1/sqrt(n), and accuracy against precision.

topics.name: And, or, not: combining chances
topics.plain: You find the chance that two things both happen, that one or the other happens, and that something happens at least once in many tries. The birthday problem uses all three.
topics.size: Chances that combine, apart from the section conditional probability takes (about 1.7 sittings on the Dewey Track), and two sections of the integrated page, which teaches not, or and and in one table. The old split into 'both' and 'either' made two half-sitting topics; the later topics use and, or and not together (the gambler's mistake is adding where he should multiply), so they merge. At least once and the birthday problem are steps: nothing outside needs them.

topics.name: Surprise and information
topics.plain: Some news tells you more than other news. A result you expected tells you little, and a surprising one tells you a lot, so both can be measured on one scale, in bits.
topics.size: Planned: no page teaches it yet. The descriptors CMPS-LO2 and CMPS-LO6 name information theory, and the earlier split made it a topic on purpose so it would not quietly drop. The nearest existing material is perplexity, on the language model page and the writing-style page.

topics.name: When one chance changes another
topics.plain: Sometimes one event changes the chance of the next, as when a card you draw is not put back in the deck. You count inside a smaller group: the chance of B, given that A happened. A medical test and the Monty Hall puzzle both depend on it.
topics.size: One section on the Dewey Track; about 1.8 sittings on the integrated course (dependence, the medical test, given which, and the Monty Hall page). Kept apart from and/or/not because it has its own formula and its own traps, and only the integrated route goes past dependence. The Monty Hall page is a step here: it is the classic puzzle of a chance that changes, and nothing needs it on its own. Needs simulation because the disease test and Monty Hall are both settled by simulating before they are counted. The closer look on two methods that agree (when-two-methods-agree) follows the Monty Hall page, so it sits here.

topics.name: Could it be luck?
topics.plain: You ask how often pure chance would give a result like the one you saw. Seven heads in ten tosses happens often with a fair coin, and seventy in a hundred almost never does. The counts of heads make the binomial distribution.
topics.size: One section on each route, under one sitting. A hidden topic: the first test of a claim against chance (a hypothesis test and a p-value, deliberately unnamed on the page) and the binomial distribution. Its own topic because it needs both combinations and simulation, and the Dewey Track teaches it before it combines chances.

topics.name: Samples, and who is missing
topics.plain: Most data covers only part of what we want to know about. You ask who collected it, how, and who is missing, because the way a sample is chosen can make some things look common and hide others.
topics.size: One section of the Statistics page, under one sitting. Small, but population, sample and sampling bias are an idea apart from any average, a learner can check it alone, and the machine learning judgement page puts it to work on training data.

topics.name: Kinds of data and frequency tables
topics.plain: Data comes in kinds: labels with no order, labels with an order, counts, and measurements. You count how often each value appears in a frequency table, and put measured numbers into equal groups, called bins, to draw a histogram, a bar for each group.
topics.size: Four sections of Kinds of data (about 1.2 sittings) or two of Statistics. The kinds of data are learned to decide how to count and draw a column (a frequency table for labels, bins for measurements); both routes teach the kinds and then the counting, back to back, and nothing needs one without the other, so one topic.

topics.name: Choosing an honest chart
topics.plain: Each chart suits one kind of question: bars and pies for categories, lines for change over time, scatter plots for two numbers together. A chart made from true numbers can still mislead, for example when a bar does not start at zero, or when two things that rise together are read as cause and effect.
topics.size: Four sections of the Dewey page and most of the integrated Charts page (listed whole: its two 'go further' sections are steps in spread): about one sitting on each route. Misleading charts come straight after choosing a chart on both routes, and nothing needs either one alone, so one topic, as the old 'Choosing a display' was. Scatter plots and correlation (with the confounder) are steps here: one section and one bullet, and nothing needs them.

topics.name: Averages, and which one to trust
topics.plain: There are three ways to say what is typical. The mean is the total divided equally among the values, the median is the middle value once the values are in order, and the mode is the most common value. A few values far from the rest pull the mean towards them, so for lopsided data the median is often the better choice.
topics.size: Both routes teach the three averages and then when they mislead, back to back: What is typical? apart from its three spread sections (about 1,500 words, one sitting), or two sections of Statistics (about 490 words). The earlier map split off 'When averages mislead', but nothing needed it, and on both routes a learner reads it before spread, so it is a step here. The Dewey page is listed whole: its other sections are the spread topic's own steps.

topics.name: Spread: range and standard deviation
topics.plain: Two sets of numbers can have the same average and still be nothing alike. The range, the standard deviation and a box plot each say how far the values spread out from the middle. Many sets of data make a bell shape, with about 68% of values within one standard deviation of the mean.
topics.size: Three sections of What is typical? (about 0.9 sittings), and spread plus percentiles and box plots on the integrated page. The range is a step: nothing needs it without the standard deviation. It needs sigma notation because the standard deviation is written with a sum, and both routes teach sigma first. Percentiles and box plots are a 'go further' step. So is the bell curve (the central limit theorem and the 68-95-99.7 rule, two optional sections of the Charts page, about 290 words): the rule is read in standard deviations, nothing needs it, and a town built from two optional sections would overstate what the site teaches.

topics.name: Simulating in time steps
topics.plain: You move a falling ball forward one short step at a time. Then you check the steps against a formula, see how shorter steps shrink the error, and see how a small error can grow over many steps.
topics.size: One page, about 1.3 sittings. The page says its real subject is how far to trust a simulation: it separates the model from the simulation of it, checks one against a formula, and shows an error that grows. Nothing is random, so it does not need the random-number topic.

topics.name: Random numbers and seeds
topics.plain: A computer makes numbers that look random but come from a calculation. You ask for them in the shape you need, pick from a list with or without repeats, and set a seed so that a run can be repeated exactly.
topics.size: One page, about 1.4 sittings. Seeds and choosing with or without replacement are taught together, and every later simulation page uses both.

topics.name: Estimating with random darts
topics.plain: You throw random points at a square and count how many land inside a shape. The share gives the shape's area, and even π. This is the Monte Carlo method: more points make the answer better, slowly, and runs can be accurate without being precise.
topics.size: One page, about 1.4 sittings, including accuracy against precision, which the time-steps page reuses. It reaches the settling idea from random numbers alone, without the probability pages, which is why it does not need Finding a chance by simulation.

topics.name: Simulating a queue
topics.plain: You simulate things arriving at random and a server clearing them. The wait grows slowly at first, then very fast as the server gets close to full. Then you ask what the model ignores, and whether that matters for your question.
topics.size: One page, about 1.2 sittings, including 'Is this a good model?', where the model is changed and checked again. Needs probability because every arrival is a chance ('arrival_prob'), and the average arrivals per step come from it.

topics.name: Markov chains: where chances settle
topics.plain: A matrix of chances for moving from one state to the next, like sunny to rainy. Multiply by it again and again, and the chances settle. The same idea chooses the next word in a sentence, and it ranked pages in the first web searches.
topics.size: One page, about one and a half sittings. It succeeds CMPS-LO4c (ranking by following links), which sits in the chance-data list; this is the page that teaches it. It sits in Simulations and models, not beside the matrices it needs: its idea is a model that moves forward by chance.

topics.name: A chain that writes
topics.plain: A program can write by choosing each next word by chance, from the words that followed the last one in a book. The counts are kept in a dictionary of dictionaries. A chain that remembers two words writes more like the book than a chain that remembers one.
topics.size: Two pages (about 2,900 words), the first series of the Machine Learning course and the text series of Computational Methods: under two sittings for a learner who carries dictionaries and functions as single ideas. Remembering more words (n-grams) is a step: nothing later needs it on its own. It does not need Markov chains: the Machine Learning course starts here with only the first Computational Methods series behind it, and the page builds its chain from scratch.

topics.name: Whose writing is it?
topics.plain: Each writer's words make a different chain. Keep some of the text back, score a passage by how likely each chain was to write it, and the better score points to the writer.
topics.size: One long page (about 2,000 words), about one and a half sittings deep in. Its own topic because the language model page starts from its held-back text and its score, and a short check can confirm it: which writer is this passage from?

topics.name: How a language model writes
topics.plain: A language model writes one piece at a time and chooses each piece by chance, like a Markov chain. You try what it does differently: a temperature, pieces smaller than words, a score for a whole passage, and numbers it learns (weights) instead of a table of counts.
topics.size: One page, about 1.1 sittings, deep in. Its six differences answer one question together, so they are steps. It needs 'Whose writing is it?' because it keeps back the same tenth of a book and turns that page's score into perplexity. The last section compares learned weights with the perceptron, but the page can be started without it.

topics.name: A model that learns from mistakes
topics.plain: A perceptron is a small model that multiplies each input by a weight and decides from the total. It is wrong at first, and it corrects its weights after each mistake. Then you test it on examples it never saw while it learned.
topics.size: One page, about 1.5 sittings: the model, training, and testing on unseen examples. Training and test examples are a step here; later pages build on them through this topic.

topics.name: Telling many kinds of picture apart
topics.plain: You build a reader for several digits from one perceptron for each digit, and take the digit with the highest total. A table of its mistakes shows which digits it confuses, and more examples make it better.
topics.size: One page, about 0.9 sittings, deep in the course, so the perceptron is carried as one idea. It adds classes, the highest-total rule and the confusion matrix, which the judgement page needs.

topics.name: Judging what a model can do
topics.plain: You test where a model fails, what its data is missing, and whose work it learned from. Then you check a claim about a model: accurate on what, compared with what, and for whom?
topics.size: One page, about 1.1 sittings. Its tests run on the digit reader and on a chain from a book, so it needs both.

topics.name: What an algorithm is
topics.plain: An algorithm is a list of clear steps, in order, that finishes a task. You can plan one in plain words, called pseudocode, before you write any code, and you can spot the ones already around you.
topics.size: About one sitting in each course: two sections of Algorithms, pseudocode and your first Python, or Recipes are algorithms with two sections of Four questions. The old list split this into three (what an algorithm is, algorithms in the real world, solving in sequence), but every page teaches them together and nothing later needs one without the others. Pseudocode stays a step: only Planning a program uses it, and it needs this whole topic.

topics.name: Your first lines of Python
topics.plain: Running a cell of Python, printing a result, and using Python as a calculator: + - * / and the three less familiar ones, // for whole divisions, % for the remainder and ** for powers.
topics.size: Under one sitting of new material, right at the very start. Each course opens with its own page (Algorithms, pseudocode and your first Python; Running Python in a cell; Four questions, with the pixel section of Numbers a computer can hold for //, % and ** on the Dewey Track), so a learner reads one route and the two closer looks on ** and //. The old list had no topic for running code at all.

topics.name: Variables: names for values
topics.plain: Giving a value a name with =, so a later line can use it. The name can be given a new value at any time, so = in Python is an instruction, not a statement that two things are equal.
topics.size: Small in words, a full sitting for a beginner, because = is where many people first get stuck. Kept apart from kinds of data because the Dewey Track teaches names on page 3 and kinds of number two pages later. The closer look on the three equals signs follows the if page, so it sits with decisions.

topics.name: Numbers, text and true or false
topics.plain: The kinds of value Python keeps: whole numbers, decimals, text, and True or False. Changing one kind into another, splitting text into its letters, asking a person to type something, and putting values into a sentence.
topics.size: Most of one median page (Variables, data types and text) for a beginner. The Dewey Track meets int and float on Numbers a computer can hold, a number page; that one section is listed here so a Dewey learner has a step too.

topics.name: Making decisions with if
topics.plain: Asking a question that is True or False, and letting the answer choose which lines run: if, elif and else, with and, or and not to join two questions into one. One equals sign gives a name a value; two ask whether two values are equal.
topics.size: One page in each course, about one sitting. The inequality sections of Choosing a path teach solving inequalities, in algebra. Joining conditions with and, or and not stays a step: the truth-table pages teach it again. The closer look on the three equals signs opens from the if page, so it sits here.

topics.name: Repeating with a for loop
topics.plain: Doing the same steps for each number from range() or each value in a list, and keeping a running total or a count as you go. A loop can hold an if, and it can hold another loop.
topics.size: About one sitting: most of Repeating steps with loops or Doing it again, and the closer look on total = 0. Split from while loops because lists, sums and grids need only this half. Loops inside loops stay a step: nothing needs them that does not also need this.

topics.name: Repeating until something changes
topics.plain: A while loop repeats its steps as long as a question is still True, so it can stop when something changes, even when nobody knows in advance how many times that will take.
topics.size: One section in each course, under a sitting even for a beginner. It is its own topic because binary search, menus that wait for 'quit' and asking again until an answer makes sense need it, while lists and sums do not.

topics.name: Sigma notation: sums written short
topics.plain: The short way mathematicians write 'add up all of these' (the Greek letter sigma, Σ) or 'multiply all of these' (pi, Π). You read one as a loop with a counter.
topics.size: One or two sections, under a sitting. The loop comes first and the notation names it afterwards, so this needs for loops. Its own topic because statistics formulas (the mean, the standard deviation) and series in other areas need the notation specifically.

topics.name: Writing functions in Python
topics.plain: Giving a group of steps a name with def, passing values in, and getting an answer from it with return. Small functions can call each other to make a bigger one.
topics.size: About one sitting: most of Writing your own functions. The Dewey Track teaches def on Recipes are algorithms and return on Numbers a computer can hold (taking a number apart), both before its first loop page, and both again on Machines that take a number, so those sections are listed here, and the topic needs only variables, not loops. Programming Foundations teaches it after loops, and its examples use them. Scope and a function's promise are split off because recursion and objects need scope, and testing and documenting need the promise, while almost everything else needs only this.

topics.name: What a Python function can see
topics.plain: Names made inside a function belong to that one call and are gone when it ends. Values go in by position or by name, and a function can see some names from outside but should not depend on them.
topics.size: Two sections for Programming Foundations; one long page (What a function can see, about two sittings) for the Dewey Track. Recursion needs 'a fresh space for every call' specifically, and methods in a class need the difference between a local name and one kept on the object.

topics.name: What a Python function promises
topics.plain: Deciding which inputs a Python function accepts and what it returns for each, what it does with an input it cannot handle, and writing that promise at the top of the function as a docstring.
topics.size: About one sitting in each course, from different pages. It joins 'an algorithm as a function on a domain of inputs' (MIT-6.2) with docstrings, because the pages teach them as one idea: the promise, and writing it down. The object course's Documenting a class is in 'Testing and documenting a class'.

topics.name: Recursion: a function that calls itself
topics.plain: A function can solve a problem by calling itself on a smaller piece of it, like counting the files in folders inside folders. It needs a case small enough to answer at once, or it never stops.
topics.size: One long page for the Dewey Track (about two sittings); one section for Computational Methods, which then walks the tree in the next topic. Split from trees because making change by trying every combination needs recursion but not trees.

topics.name: Lists: many values in order
topics.plain: Keeping many values under one name, in order. Reaching one by its position, counting from 0, taking a slice, changing a value, adding two lists, and visiting a list one position at a time.
topics.size: One page in Programming Foundations; one long page (about two sittings) in the Dewey Track. Going through a list by position (the old 'iterating by index') and adding lists element by element (the old 'arrays') are sections of these pages, and nothing needs them apart from lists.

topics.name: List comprehensions, grids and copies
topics.plain: A comprehension builds a list in one line, a grid keeps rows and columns as a list of lists, and a copy stops two names from sharing one list. The dot product multiplies two lists pair by pair and adds the results.
topics.size: One page, Comprehensions, grids and aliasing (about 2,000 words, a sitting and a half), and the closer look on two names for one list. The earlier map cut it into three towns of 340 to 1,200 words at depths 6 and 7. Later pages cite the page as one unit, each for a different part (Leaving it to chance for the comprehension, the matrix pages for grids, the aliasing trap and the dot product, the debugging pages for the copy), and deep in, one page of this size is one topic. It needs writing functions because its later sections (inside a function, sequences as functions, the dot product) define and pass functions. The dot product is a step here: Multiplying grids teaches it again, and the perceptron needs this whole topic anyway.

topics.name: Dictionaries: looking up by name
topics.plain: Keeping values under names, called keys, instead of positions, so a program can look one up, change it, check whether a key is there, or count how often things happen.
topics.size: One median page, one sitting. The old list had no topic for dictionaries, though classes, folder trees, maps, word chains and the cache in 'making change' all build on them. The Dewey Track has no dictionaries page; it meets them on the frequency-table section of Kinds of data, so that section is a step here too.

topics.name: Searching: linear and binary search
topics.plain: Finding one value in a list: look at every item in turn, or, when the list is sorted, look only in the half where the value must be, again and again. Halving is why the second way is so fast.
topics.size: One page in each course (about two sittings in the Dewey Track). Divide and conquer is named on these pages, after binary search; the only other use is bisection, which builds on binary search, so it is a step here and not a topic.

topics.name: Sorting a list
topics.plain: Putting a list in order one swap at a time: selection sort, insertion sort and bubble sort, and Python's own sorted(), with a key when the order is not the obvious one.
topics.size: One page in each course, one to two sittings. Comparing the sorts' speed is split off into the next topic, where the Dewey Track gives it a whole page.

topics.name: How work grows with size
topics.plain: Judging an algorithm by how its steps grow as the input grows, not by one small example: in step with the size, by halvings, by the square, or faster still. The best case, the usual case and the worst case can differ.
topics.size: One page (Racing the sorts) for the Dewey Track; a section of Putting things in order for Programming Foundations, Computational Methods and the integrated course. Counting looks and comparisons stays inside searching and sorting, where it is the reason to care; this topic names the pattern afterwards. The growth section of Three ways to make change reads that page's own tables, so it stays with the strategies topic.

topics.name: Searching folder trees and maps
topics.plain: Some structures branch, like folders inside folders, and some join in loops, like streets on a map. You visit every part, either down one branch to its end first (depth first) or one level at a time (breadth first), and find the shortest way between two places.
topics.size: Two consecutive pages in Computational Methods, about two sittings. Trees and graphs are one topic because they are always taught together and nothing needs one without the other: the map search reuses the tree's breadth-first walk. Graphs were never named in the old list.

topics.name: Three strategies for hard problems
topics.plain: Three ways to attack a hard problem: try every possibility, remember answers you have already found, or take the best-looking step each time and accept an answer that may not be the best.
topics.size: Most of one long page, about one and a half sittings. It needs recursion (brute force calls itself), dictionaries (the cache) and how work grows (choosing a strategy weighs speed against certainty).

topics.name: Classes and objects
topics.plain: A class is a blueprint that says what an object has (its fields) and what it can do (its methods). An object is one thing built from that blueprint, with its own values, and its methods use the same moves as any program: storing, order, choices and loops.
topics.size: The first two pages of the object course, about one and a half sittings. The course starts from a list of dictionaries and asks why that is not enough, so dictionaries come first.

topics.name: Keeping an object's rules inside it
topics.plain: Putting the rules about an object's data in its methods, so every caller meets them, and keeping the data behind those methods. Giving the class more methods that use each other, and values that every object of the class shares.
topics.size: Two pages, about two sittings. A class with many methods goes here, not with classes and objects, because it builds on the encapsulated class from the page before it ('your class, second version') and nothing else needs it on its own.

topics.name: Designing classes from a description
topics.plain: Reading a description written in words and deciding which classes a program needs, what each one is responsible for, and which others it works with, before any code is written.
topics.size: One page, one sitting. A skill of its own that a short check can confirm: given a description, name the classes, their jobs and their partners. It needs encapsulation: one of its three questions is 'Does it keep a rule? ... it belongs to the submarine, as it did on Encapsulation', its classes keep their data behind an underscore, and your game answer put organising data (FOOP-LO8) before modelling (FOOP-LO7).

topics.name: One class built from others
topics.plain: Building a new class on one it is a kind of (inheritance), or giving a class objects of other classes to hold (composition), and deciding which fits: 'is a' or 'has a'.
topics.size: Two pages and a closer look, about two sittings. Merged because they are always taught together, the closer look is about choosing between them, and nothing needs one without the other.

topics.name: Testing and documenting a class
topics.plain: You test a class with many small tests, one for each thing it promises, and write a test before you fix a bug. Then you write those promises down as docstrings on the class and each method, with examples that Python can check.
topics.size: Two pages of the object course (about 1,900 words, a sitting and a half), the last two before its front end and its capstone. Both work on the same world's classes: the testing page opens with five versions of the submarine from Inheritance and copies the classes from Composition, and the documenting page continues from it. In the earlier map they were steps in 'Testing that code works' and 'What a function promises', which need no classes, so a learner could reach a page about subclasses they had never met. The testing page uses assert without explaining it, so it needs 'Testing that code works'. The documenting page says the learner 'may have met' docstrings on functions, so 'What a Python function promises' is not a need.

topics.name: Reading an error message
topics.plain: When Python stops, it tells you the kind of error, the line, and the trail of calls that led there, called the traceback. Some errors come before a program starts, some while it runs, and some mistakes give no error at all.
topics.size: One page in each course (Reading an error message, or When Python says no), one to two sittings. The two pages are alternatives, so the effort table counts this topic twice over.

topics.name: Finding a bug and its cause
topics.plain: When a program goes wrong, you find the line that causes it: read the traceback, print values at the right moment, follow the code by hand or with a debugger, make the example smaller, and fix the cause, not only the symptom. A code editor helps, by finishing names and showing what they are.
topics.size: One idea on four routes, about one sitting each: Finding bugs in bigger programs (Programming Foundations), two sections of Does it work? (the Dewey Track), Debugging: from a report to the line that caused it (Computational Methods), and the object course's page on the development environment. The earlier map kept the Computational Methods page apart as 'Tracking a bug to its cause', but Finding bugs in bigger programs also starts from a wrong answer with no error, no course teaches both, nothing needs either, and a teacher could not tell the two towns apart by name. It needs lists because the Programming Foundations page opens with errors from lists and dictionaries. The object course's page finds its bug inside a class, so it is an 'applies' step, except its two sections on the editor and the Notebook, which are the site's only teaching of a development environment (FOOP-LO5).

topics.name: Testing that code works
topics.plain: Checking code against inputs whose answers you already know, with assert, including unusual inputs at the edges and answers that are only close enough. Many tests run together, and a test written before a fix.
topics.size: A section or a page in each course, about one sitting. The object course's page on testing a class starts from the submarines of Inheritance, so it is in 'Testing and documenting a class', which needs this topic and classes.

topics.name: Code other people can read
topics.plain: Names, comments and layout that let somebody else, or you in a month, understand code without asking. Reviewing someone's code with a checklist, and changing code without changing what it does.
topics.size: One and a half to two sittings for the Dewey Track, under one for Programming Foundations. Code review stays a step: nothing needs it apart from readable code, and both courses teach the two together.

topics.name: A program someone else can use
topics.plain: Turning code in cells into a program that runs from start to end, asks a person what to do, continues until they choose to stop, copes when they type something unexpected, and runs outside this website.
topics.size: Most of one page, From cells to a program, about one sitting. A front end for a class puts the same moves (a menu loop, checking input, keeping the deciding apart from the asking) to work on the object course's classes, and opens where Documenting a class ends, so it is an 'applies' step here.

topics.name: Planning a program in releases
topics.plain: Deciding what a first version will do before you write code, planning its steps and its functions, agreeing what 'done' means, and building it in small releases that each work.
topics.size: About one sitting of teaching, then weeks of doing. Split from team work because the solo project (A program of your own) needs planning and releases and no team.

topics.name: How programming languages differ
topics.plain: What changes from one language to the next, and what stays the same: machine code, assembly and languages people can read, compilers and interpreters, and different ways of organising a program.
topics.size: One page in each course, one to two sittings. The history in these pages is a landmark (PDP-LO1 is culled); the binary and hexadecimal sections of How programming languages came to be are steps in those two topics. The section of When Python says no on compilers and linkers is about reading errors on a page from the Dewey Track's first unit, so it stays with 'Reading an error message'.

topics.name: Choosing a code editor
topics.plain: An editor is a program for changing the plain text files a website is made of. You can install one, such as VS Code, or use the one on GitHub's website with nothing to install.
topics.size: One short page for a beginner. Kept apart from forking because Database Methods and Issues and pull requests use the editor without the starter copy.

topics.name: A GitHub account
topics.plain: GitHub is a website that keeps projects, called repositories, where other people can see them and work on them. You make a free account, and your username becomes part of your site's address.
topics.size: One short page with no cells (about 830 words), the first page of both Database Methods and Web Authoring. A topic rather than an orientation landmark because making your own copy of a project and filing an issue both need an account and the idea of a repository, and no other page teaches what GitHub is for.

topics.name: Issues and pull requests
topics.plain: Two ways people work together on a project on GitHub: an issue reports a problem in the open, and a pull request proposes a change for somebody else to review.
topics.size: One short page with no cells, near the start of the web and database courses: small, as a beginner topic should be. The old list never named Git or GitHub. The other Git pages (how Git keeps history, commit and push, forks) are in the web area.

topics.name: Your own copy of a project
topics.plain: Making your own copy of another person's repository on GitHub, as a fork or from a template, and choosing how to open it: in the browser, as a download, or as a clone.
topics.size: One short page. Publishing needs it, and the project starter repeats it as a landmark, so it stands on its own.

topics.name: How Git keeps history
topics.plain: What a commit holds, why git add comes before git commit, and how the commits of a project form a history you can read, on your own computer and on GitHub.
topics.size: A context page made a topic: it teaches Git itself (snapshots, the staging area, history, branches), which the brief names as a hidden topic and which pull requests and forks lean on. About one sitting.

topics.name: Making a table in SQL
topics.plain: A database keeps its data in tables, with one row for each thing and one column for each fact about it. One column, the primary key, gives every row its own value. Three SQL statements make a table, add rows to it and show what it holds.
topics.size: One long first page (about 1,800 words, two cells): what a table and a database are, where databases show up, then CREATE TABLE, INSERT and SELECT *, data types, an automatic primary key and the _tbl naming rule. It is one activity, building one table and reading it back, and nothing later needs the words 'row' and 'column' without the statements that make them, so the old split into tables, statements and 'where databases show up' is merged. Where databases show up is a section, not an idea of its own.

topics.name: Filtering and sorting rows
topics.plain: Asking a table for only the columns and rows you want, with a condition after WHERE, and putting the answer in order with ORDER BY.
topics.size: One beginner page (about 1,050 words): naming columns, WHERE with the six comparisons, ORDER BY ASC and DESC. UPDATE and DELETE need WHERE but not ORDER BY, yet ORDER BY on its own is a few paragraphs that nothing needs by itself, so it stays a step here rather than a topic. 'SQL as a query language' was never taught apart from writing these queries, so its old topic folds in here.

topics.name: Changing and deleting rows
topics.plain: Changing values in rows that are already there with UPDATE, and removing rows with DELETE, without changing more rows than you meant to.
topics.size: One beginner page (about 830 words). It is its own topic because joins, design and the data pages all need filtering but none needs UPDATE or DELETE. It needs WHERE: both statements pick their rows with one, and the page's main lesson is what happens without it.

topics.name: Counting and averaging rows
topics.plain: Asking a table for one number about many rows: how many there are, their average, or the largest.
topics.size: Planned: COUNT, AVG and GROUP BY have no teaching page yet; see the gaps question. Exercise 5 of SQL practice puts COUNT(*) to work, with the answer in its hint. The Dewey Track runs AVG, COUNT(*) and MAX on Many languages, one idea, to show that SQL is declarative; that section stays with 'How programming languages differ', whose idea it is, and whose learners have not met WHERE. Counting and totals are among the first things a learner asks a real table, so the town stays on the map, marked planned, like 'Surprise and information'.

topics.name: Joining two tables
topics.plain: Keeping two kinds of thing in two tables. A column in one table, a foreign key, holds the other table's primary key, and JOIN combines the matching rows in one query.
topics.size: One short beginner page (about 740 words): why data is split into two tables, the foreign key, JOIN ... ON and table.column. The two context sections of 'Sets in databases' (a number-area context page) show a JOIN as every pair of rows, then only the pairs that match; they are side reading, not a need. Kept apart from LEFT JOIN because design, the timetable and the library quiz all need a plain JOIN and never LEFT JOIN.

topics.name: When a join drops rows
topics.plain: A JOIN keeps only the rows whose values match exactly. LEFT JOIN keeps every row from the first table and leaves a gap where there was no match, so you can see which rows had no partner.
topics.size: A hidden topic: one short page (about 510 words) on a real dataset, where 'USA' and 'United States' never meet, then LEFT JOIN, then fixing the spelling. It is smaller than one sitting, but it is a distinct idea a learner names (inner and outer joins), and nothing later needs it, so folding it into 'Joining two tables' would make every later topic wait for it. The first cell reloads the CSV table from the loading page, but a learner can run it without that topic, so it is not a need.

topics.name: Designing a database
topics.plain: Deciding what tables a problem needs, what one row of each one is, which columns are primary keys, and which are foreign keys that point at other tables. Then building those tables in SQL.
topics.size: One page and two sections, about 1,600 words: one kind of thing per table, a column type for every column, one-to-many links and the entity relationship diagram, then the timetable's five-table design (four tables of things, one of events), dates written so they sort, FOREIGN KEY ... REFERENCES, dropping tables in reverse order and the doubled quote. Designing and building are merged because they are always taught together and nothing needs the design without the build. It needs a plain JOIN: the join is the concrete reason to split tables, and the design page names what the join page already did.

topics.name: Many-to-many links
topics.plain: When a book can have several authors and an author several books, a third table holds the pairs: one row for each book and author that belong together.
topics.size: A hidden topic, taught only inside the library loans quiz: the junction table and a primary key made of two columns (task 2), filling it so one book has two authors and one author two books (task 4), and joining through it and across three tables, with IS NULL for a loan not yet returned (task 6). About one sitting deep in the course. The rest of the quiz is building practice, so the page is also a project landmark.

topics.name: Joining a table to itself
topics.plain: Joining several tables in one query, and comparing a table's rows with each other under two names, for example to find two bookings of one room at the same time.
topics.size: A hidden topic: the query half of the timetable page, about 1,100 words. It covers three JOINs in one query with AS names for columns, the overlap test (each session starts before the other ends), the self-join with two names for one table, and s1.session_id < s2.session_id to skip a row matched with itself. It needs 'Designing a database' because it queries the five tables that topic designs and builds; the design and build half of the same page is that topic's last two steps.

topics.name: The query behind a form
topics.plain: When someone presses submit on a form, their answers become the values in one INSERT. The database adds them to a table as a new row.
topics.size: One short page (about 500 words, one cell), close to the start in what it needs: only INSERT and an automatic key. It stays a topic because it is the one place the course connects a database to a form, and the web area's Full Stack page takes it further (a visitor's typed text filling a ? placeholder in a query). That page is listed as 'applies', not 'teaches', because it also needs JavaScript, which this page does not.

topics.name: Loading real data into a table
topics.plain: Reading a file of real data into Python as a table, tidying its column names and checking what is missing, and then writing it into the database so SQL can ask it questions.
topics.size: Two pages, about 1,470 words, one sitting.
