The first is a hidden idea (pandas and the DataFrame: a table in Python, filtered the way WHERE filters), but it exists to prepare the second ('To do that, Python needs a table of its own'), they are always taught together, and nothing in this area needs a DataFrame without the CSV: the sharing pages need both. So they merge. Needs filtering because the pandas page teaches its filter as the Python form of WHERE, and the loading page ends with a SELECT.

topics.name: A page that reads a database
topics.plain: A page's own script sends a query to a database and turns each row of the result into part of the page. A placeholder keeps a visitor's typed text out of the query itself.
topics.size: The one Full Stack page, short but deep: the learner brings SQL and HTML as single ideas. Split into rows and search it would be two tiny topics, so one.

topics.name: Sharing a query's result
topics.plain: Bringing a query's answer into Python, and then showing it as a line chart or saving it as a CSV file that someone else can open in a spreadsheet.
topics.size: Two short pages (about 430 and 400 words). Both start the same way, read_sql turning a query's result into a DataFrame (the reverse of to_sql), and then one draws a chart and one writes a CSV. Apart, each would be half a sitting deep in the course; together they are one sitting, nothing needs one without the other, and the old topic already held both. Needs the loading topic for the DataFrame, to_sql and the CSV shape it reverses.

topics.name: HTML tags: your first web page
topics.plain: A web page is a plain text file. Tags mark what each piece of text is, and an attribute adds detail to a tag. Every page has a head, for facts about the page, and a body, for what a visitor sees.
topics.size: Two very short pages, under one sitting together. Everything later needs both, and they are always taught one after the other, so one topic.

topics.name: Headings and tags that describe content
topics.plain: Choosing a tag for what the content is, not for how it looks: heading levels, strong and em, and containers such as nav, header, main and section.
topics.size: Two short pages, about one sitting. Both teach the same idea, meaning over looks, and nothing needs one without the other.

topics.name: Placing an image
topics.plain: The img tag puts a picture on a page. Its src attribute says where the file is, and figure and figcaption add a caption under it.
topics.size: One page, shared with file-paths: its 'two kinds of address' section is the start of that topic. Alt text, image sizes and flexible images all need it.

topics.name: Form fields and labels
topics.plain: A label names a form field, and its for attribute joins it to the field's id. type="email" and required check an answer before the form is sent.
topics.size: One very short page, early enough to stay small. Sending a form and the full-stack search box both need it.

topics.name: Paths: finding a file
topics.plain: A path is the address of a file inside your own site, starting from the page that uses it. A slash goes into a folder, two dots go up one folder, and capital letters count.
topics.size: A hidden topic. Two sections, small, but links, stylesheets and an images folder all need paths without needing img, so the split test makes it its own topic.

topics.name: Links and menus
topics.plain: An a tag makes a link to another page, another site, an email address, or a place further down the same page. A menu is a list of links inside a nav tag.
topics.size: Two short pages, about one sitting. Nothing later needs links without menus or menus without links, and they are taught one after the other.

topics.name: CSS rules, selectors and classes
topics.plain: A CSS rule has a selector, which chooses elements, and declarations, which say how they look. A stylesheet holds the rules for many pages, and a class lets a rule reach only some elements.
topics.size: Two short pages, about one sitting. Almost every CSS page after the first uses class selectors, so nothing needs rules without selectors.

topics.name: Colours and CSS variables
topics.plain: Writing a colour as a name or a hex code, and storing a value once in a CSS variable so that many rules can use it.
topics.size: One page. Its last section, the contrast check, is also the first step of colour-contrast. BEM needs the variables and contrast needs the colours.

topics.name: The box model: padding, border, margin
topics.plain: Every element is a box with three layers around its content: padding, a border and a margin. Two margins that meet can join into one.
topics.size: One page. The page width topic and flexbox both need it on its own.

topics.name: Text size and units
topics.plain: Measuring sizes in px or rem, how rem follows the root font size, and placing text on the left, the right or the centre with text-align.
topics.size: One page. Colour contrast needs it (text a reader can make bigger), and nothing needs it with the box model, so it stands alone.

topics.name: Which rule wins: the cascade
topics.plain: When two rules set the same thing on one element, the more precise selector wins, and between equal selectors the later rule wins. Some properties, such as colour, pass down to the elements inside.
topics.size: A context page made a topic: the cascade, specificity and inheritance are a hidden topic the brief names, and no tutorial teaches them. A long page, one to two sittings.

topics.name: Naming classes so they stay tidy
topics.plain: BEM is a pattern for class names: block, element and modifier. A class name then says what it is for, and a modifier class can change one variable for one part of the page.
topics.size: One page, a little deeper in. It needs variables for its scoped override; nothing needs it.

topics.name: A header that stays in view
topics.plain: The position property changes how an element moves as the page scrolls. With position: sticky and top: 0, a header stays at the top.
topics.size: One page, with the layout page's section on all five values of position as background.

topics.name: Media queries: layouts for phones
topics.plain: CSS that applies only when a condition is true, usually a screen width. A breakpoint is the width where the layout changes, and a phone needs one line in the head, the viewport meta tag, to use its real width.
topics.size: One page, with its background page on the viewport tag, mobile-first and choosing breakpoints. Grid and the site menu need it without flexible images, so the two stay apart.

topics.name: Images that fit the screen
topics.plain: Two declarations, max-width: 100% and height: auto, let an image shrink to fit a narrow screen and keep its shape.
topics.size: One short page. It cannot join media queries (grid needs those without it) or images (it needs CSS), so it is a small topic of its own.

topics.name: Centring content and placing footers
topics.plain: Stopping content from growing too wide with max-width, centring it with auto margins, and keeping a footer at the bottom of a short page.
topics.size: Two pages, about one sitting. Both use an auto margin to take the leftover space, and the footer page says so. Nothing needs the footer on its own, so it is a step here.

topics.name: Flexbox: boxes in a row
topics.plain: display: flex puts boxes side by side in a row, which can wrap onto a new line. Grow, shrink and basis decide how the boxes share the space.
topics.size: Two pages, one to two sittings. The second only takes apart flex: 1 1 80px from the first, so they are one idea. A hidden topic the old list swallowed into 'Styling pages with CSS'.

topics.name: Grid: rows and columns
topics.plain: display: grid places boxes in rows and columns at once. Named areas describe a whole page as a small map, and auto-fit lets a grid choose its own number of columns.
topics.size: Two pages, about one sitting, with the flexbox-or-grid comparison as background. The named-areas page swaps its map inside a media query.

topics.name: Screen order and HTML order
topics.plain: The order property moves a box on screen, but the Tab key and screen readers still follow the HTML. When the order matters, change the HTML instead.
topics.size: One page. It needs a flex row and the idea of keyboard focus; nothing needs it.

topics.name: Hover and focus
topics.plain: Styling a button while a pointer is over it, and while the keyboard has reached it. A transition on the button's own rule makes the change smooth both ways.
topics.size: One page. Transforms, screen order and keyboard accessibility all start from it.

topics.name: Transforms and transitions: moving smoothly
topics.plain: transform moves, resizes or turns an element without moving anything around it. transition makes a change happen smoothly, over a set time.
topics.size: One page. Kept apart from keyframes because the checkbox hack needs transitions but not keyframes.

topics.name: Animation with keyframes
topics.plain: A @keyframes rule names the stages of an animation, and the animation property says how long it takes and how often it repeats. It needs no trigger.
topics.size: One short page. 3D in CSS needs it on its own.

topics.name: Opening and closing with a checkbox
topics.plain: A hidden checkbox, a label joined to it, and a :checked rule can show and hide content with no JavaScript. HTML's own details element does the same job, and works with a keyboard.
topics.size: One page, with details and summary from the accessibility page as background.

topics.name: Depth and 3D in CSS
topics.plain: perspective gives a flat page depth, so nearer things look bigger. With rotateY and translateZ, flat boxes can circle a sun or make a turning cube, and the order of the transforms matters.
topics.size: Three pages, about two and a half sittings, deep in the course where transforms and keyframes are carried as single ideas. The cube teaches transform order and the ball uses it at once, so they stay together.

topics.name: Drawing frames on a canvas
topics.plain: A canvas is a rectangle of pixels that JavaScript draws on. An animation loop clears it, moves things a little, draws them again and asks for the next frame. Far things are drawn first.
topics.size: Two pages, one and a half sittings, deep in. The cube page reuses the first page's loop and projection, and nothing needs the first without the second. It does by hand what 3D in CSS let the browser do, so that comes first.

topics.name: Looking inside a page: the inspector
topics.plain: A tool built into every browser that shows the HTML and CSS behind a page, lists the rules that affect each part, and shows errors from loading it.
topics.size: One page, taught before any HTML. Many later pages (the cascade, layout, the footer, flexbox or grid, troubleshooting) open it.

topics.name: Publishing a site with GitHub Pages
topics.plain: GitHub Pages turns the files in a repository into a real website, free, at an address like username.github.io/repository-name. The home page must be a file called index.html.
topics.size: One short page for a beginner; the two loops and fetching a page both start from a published site.

topics.name: Saving and publishing a change
topics.plain: Two loops you repeat all the time. On your computer you save a file and refresh the browser. On GitHub you commit, push and wait a minute for the site to rebuild.
topics.size: One page. It is the working habit every later 'now in your own site' section uses, and Git history and troubleshooting build on it.

topics.name: Fixing a broken web page
topics.plain: The checks that find the usual problems: a blank page, a stylesheet that does nothing, an image that will not show, an unclosed tag or brace, and a change that does not appear.
topics.size: The web sections of one reference page, about one sitting. Its SQL and 'this site' sections are not web ideas and are left off. A skill a short check can confirm: find the mistake in a broken page.

topics.name: How a browser reads HTML
topics.plain: A browser reads an HTML file from top to bottom and builds a tree of elements, each one inside another. It fixes small mistakes, treats several spaces as one, and skips comments.
topics.size: A context page made a topic: the document tree, void elements and character references are taught nowhere else, and the tree is what the inspector, selectors and the accessibility tree all show. About one sitting.

topics.name: How a browser fetches a page
topics.plain: What happens between typing a web address and seeing the page: finding the right computer, asking it for each file, getting a reply, and keeping copies for next time.
topics.size: A context page made a topic: addresses, DNS, requests, responses and the cache are how a browser works, and sending a form needs the idea of a request to a server. About one sitting.

topics.name: How a browser places boxes
topics.plain: Where a browser puts each box when no layout rule moves it: block boxes stack and inline boxes wrap like words. It also covers what width measures, and every value of position.
topics.size: A context page made a topic: normal flow, display, box-sizing, position: absolute and z-index are taught nowhere else, and later layout (flexbox's box-sizing, absolute boxes in 3D) draws on them. A long page, one to two sittings.

topics.name: Where a form's answers go
topics.plain: When a form is sent, the browser sends each field's name and answer to an address the form names. A server must be there to receive them, and it has to check every answer again.
topics.size: A context page made a topic: name/value pairs, get and post, servers and validation are taught nowhere else, and Database Methods' form-to-a-row page leans on them. About one sitting.

topics.name: How a browser draws each frame
topics.plain: A screen shows many still pictures a second. For each one the browser finds the styles, places the boxes, then paints them, which is why some movement is smoother than other movement.
topics.size: A context page made a topic, the last part of how a browser works. About one sitting. It explains requestAnimationFrame and speed on fast screens from the canvas pages, so it comes after them.

topics.name: Screen readers and search engines
topics.plain: Other readers use a page's HTML, not its picture. A screen reader reads the page aloud from the accessibility tree, a list of the page's parts that the browser builds, and a search engine reads the same meaning.
topics.size: A context page made a topic: it is the reason behind every semantic choice in the HTML series, and accessibility is a hidden topic the brief names. About one sitting.

topics.name: Describing images with alt text
topics.plain: The alt attribute describes an image in words, for a screen reader or for a picture that fails to load. An empty alt tells a screen reader to skip a decoration.
topics.size: One page. Its own skill, what makes a good description, which a short check can confirm.

topics.name: Colour contrast and text size
topics.plain: A contrast ratio says how easy text is to read on its background, and the web's accessibility guidelines ask for at least 4.5 to 1. Readers who make their text bigger need sizes in rem, not px.
topics.size: The contrast check on the colours page, then its background page, which names the ratio and adds rgb(), hsl() and text size. About one sitting. Made a topic because contrast is the accessibility idea a finished design is checked against.

topics.name: Keyboards, focus and movement
topics.plain: Using a page with the keyboard alone, keeping the focus outline visible, treating hover as an extra, and giving less movement to people who ask their device for it.
topics.size: A context page made a topic: tab order, :focus-visible, the skip link and prefers-reduced-motion are taught nowhere else. One and a half sittings. It discusses the checkbox hack's weakness and turning animations off, so it needs both.

topics.name: Image formats and file size
topics.plain: JPEG suits a photo, PNG suits a screenshot or a logo, and SVG suits flat shapes. Resizing and compressing a photo can make its file many times smaller, so the page loads fast.
topics.size: Two sections of a short page, with a full background page on pixels and compression. About one sitting. The design principle of access speed.

topics.name: Planning and documenting a site
topics.plain: Before building, a site map says what each page is for and how the pages connect, and a wireframe sketches each layout. Afterwards, a README says what you built, and a maintenance plan says how to keep it current.
topics.size: Two short pages, about one sitting. They are the two halves of one job, the documents that go with a site: the documenting page opens by setting its README beside the plan.

topics.name: One menu across a whole site
topics.plain: The same menu, in the same order, on every page, with the attribute aria-current telling a screen reader which page you are on. On a phone, the links stack into one column.
topics.size: Two very short pages, under one sitting, both about the site's menu. Each alone would be far too small at this depth, and nothing needs either.

topics.name: Decimals, percentages and ratio
topics.plain: Three more ways to write part of a whole: as a decimal, as a percentage, and as a ratio that compares two amounts. Each can be turned into the others.
topics.size: Planned: no page teaches it yet (Josh, 28 September 2026: a planned town for every gap).

topics.name: Multiplying negative numbers
topics.plain: What happens to the sign when you multiply or divide with negative numbers, and why a negative times a negative is positive.
topics.size: Planned: no page teaches it yet (Josh, 28 September 2026: a planned town for every gap).

topics.name: Kinds of triangle
topics.plain: Triangles named by their sides and their angles: equilateral, isosceles, scalene and right-angled. Knowing which kind you have tells you which rules you can use.
topics.size: Planned: no page teaches it yet (Josh, 28 September 2026: a planned town for every gap).

topics.name: Lists and tables in HTML
topics.plain: Marking up a list of items, and a table of rows and columns, so that a browser and a screen reader both know what they are.
topics.size: Planned: no page teaches it yet (Josh, 28 September 2026: a planned town for every gap).

topics.name: Comparing rows of numbers
topics.plain: Treating a row of numbers as a point, measuring how far apart two rows are, and finding the nearest one. It is how a program finds things that are like each other.
topics.size: Planned: no page teaches it yet (Josh, 28 September 2026: a planned town for every gap).

questions.q: The map has eleven regions, the top of the range. Four are judgement calls. 'Logic and binary' (8 topics: binary, hexadecimal, floats, XOR and parity, sets, Venn diagrams, truth tables, De Morgan) stands apart from Number, although strands.yaml put sets and logic in 'Sets and number systems'. 'Machine learning' (6 topics, the whole Machine Learning course) stands apart from Chance and data. The web is two regions, 'Building web pages' (HTML, CSS, layout, movement: 25 topics) and 'Websites and browsers' (21 topics), which now also holds 'Your tools: an editor and GitHub', because those pages are the first week of Web Authoring and Database Methods and no programming course uses them. That move leaves 'Making software' with two districts and 8 topics (reading errors, finding bugs, testing; readable code, programs for users, planning, languages, team work).
options: Eleven regions as drawn
Fold Making software into Programming (eight districts, 33 topics)
Fold Logic and binary into Number (six districts, 31 topics)
Fold Machine learning into Chance and data as one district
One web region with fewer, larger districts
questions.lean: Eleven as drawn. At the first zoom only region names show, so a learner looking for testing, binary, truth tables or machine learning finds them by name. Making software is small, but testing, debugging and working in a team are what the Working in a Team series and half the object course are about, and inside Programming they would sit among loops and lists.

questions.q: Ten web context pages are topics here, not context steps: the cascade, how Git keeps history, the four 'How a browser…' pages, who reads a page, colour contrast, keyboards and movement, and where a form's answers go (and, in number, how a computer stores a number, as 'Why 0.1 + 0.2 is not 0.3'). Each teaches an idea no tutorial teaches, and the brief names the cascade, Git, how a browser works and accessibility as hidden topics. But most are leaves: each such page says you do not need it to finish its owner page, so almost nothing needs them.
options: Keep them as topics (as drawn)
Make them context steps in their owners' topics, and keep topics only for tutorial pages
Keep only the ideas the brief names (the cascade, Git, how a browser works, accessibility) and fold colour contrast and sending a form into their owners
questions.lean: Keep them as topics. A learner looks for 'the cascade' or 'how a browser fetches a page' on the map; as context steps they would be hidden inside towns named for something else.
questions.answer: Keep the context pages as towns.

questions.q: decisions.yaml records your pair answer that truth tables come before Venn diagrams (MIT-2.4 before MIT-2.3). The Dewey Venn page reminds the reader of XOR ('exactly one') and of 2ⁿ rows, but the integrated course teaches Venn diagrams before truth tables, and its Venn page stands alone. The map has no need between them.
options: No need (as drawn)
Venn diagrams need truth tables
questions.lean: No need. The Dewey reminders are ones a learner can do without, and the integrated course shows the diagrams work first.

questions.q: Your game answer put 'Multiplying out to quadratics' (MIT-1.8) before the derivative (MIT-3.6). All four derivative pages find slopes with numbers (derivative_at) and never expand (x + h)². The map has the derivative needing limits and the slope of a line only.
options: No need on expanding brackets (as drawn)
The derivative needs expanding brackets
questions.lean: No need. The pages as written do not expand, so the edge would close a door for nothing. If a page later derives 2x from (x + h)², the edge comes back.

questions.q: Should 'Kinds of data' come before averages? decisions.yaml says yes (MIT-5.9 before MIT-5.12 and MIT-5.13, 'settled, after going round twice'). Both courses teach averages first (What is typical? before Kinds of data; Statistics' averages before its data types section), and the kinds are motivated by which average is allowed, which is discover first. The map has no need either way.
options: No need either way (as drawn)
Kinds of data before averages, as decided before
Averages before kinds of data, as both courses teach it
questions.lean: No need either way. Neither is needed to start the other; making either one a need closes a door that both courses show is open.

questions.q: decisions.yaml splits MIT-5.8 into 'Combining with and', 'Combining with or' and 'Conditional probability'. The map has two topics: and, or and not together (with 'at least once' and the birthday problem as steps), and conditional probability apart.
options: Two topics (as drawn)
Three topics, as decided before: and, or, conditional
Four: and, or, at least once, conditional
questions.lean: Two. Split three ways, 'both' and 'either' are about half a sitting each, and the later topics use them together. Conditional probability has its own formula and traps, and only the integrated route goes past dependence.

questions.q: Team programming (PDP-LO12): a topic, or metadata for the teacher's view? design.md's example culls it as keeping evidence. Building it together teaches roles, written agreements about whose code calls whose, releases, reviews, a definition of done and a retrospective.
options: A topic, 'Building software as a team' (as drawn)
Culled as metadata, with the team briefs as landmarks
questions.lean: A topic. Those practices are things a learner can show; only 'teams of three to five' and the evidence are course requirements.
questions.answer: Teacher-only metadata: the town comes off the map; the team briefs are landmarks.

questions.q: Most maths and programming topics have two to four alternative teaching routes, one per course, and the revision added more: 'Finding a bug and its cause' now holds four courses' pages, 'Writing functions in Python' no longer needs loops because the Dewey Track teaches def and return before its loop page (while Programming Foundations' page uses loops in its examples), and 'Letters for numbers' gains a Dewey section from a functions page. Steps carry no needs, so a learner who opens a town sees every route, including pages that assume another course's order. The validator's effort table also adds the routes together: its median at depths 5 to 11 is about 2,100 to 4,500 words, where one learner on one route reads about 2,000 to 2,950.
options: Yes: tag each step with its courses, and show a learner the steps on their own route first
No: steps in reading order are enough
questions.lean: Tag them. layout.py already computes each page's courses; carrying them onto steps lets a town show 'your route' first, keeps a Programming Foundations learner out of the object course's class pages, and makes the size check honest.
questions.answer: Yes: tag each step with its courses.

questions.q: Several ideas a learner would expect have no page yet: decimals, percentages and ratio (MIT-1.1 names operations in Q and R); multiplying and dividing negative numbers (MIT-1.1's operations in Z; the number line page only adds and takes away, yet inverse functions, complex numbers and inequalities all assume that a negative times a negative is positive); kinds of triangle (old PRE-1, folded into Pythagoras); information theory (CMPS-LO2 and CMPS-LO6); counting and grouping rows in SQL (COUNT is only in a practice hint, GROUP BY nowhere); HTML lists and tables (the Full Stack page uses a table without explaining it); vectors and nearest-neighbour search (CMPS-LO4d, culled to metadata). Two of these are on the map as planned towns with no teaching page: 'Surprise and information' and, since this revision, 'Counting and averaging rows', whose two borrowed steps did not teach it.
options: Keep the two planned towns and list the other gaps in a planning note
Add a planned town for every gap (a planned 'Multiplying negative numbers' would sit in Number basics, needing the number line)
Take the planned towns off too, and list every gap in a planning note
questions.lean: Keep the two planned towns, and write two pages first: GROUP BY, because totals per group are among the first things a learner asks a real table, and multiplying negatives, because four later towns already lean on it.
questions.answer: A planned town for every gap.

questions.q: everything-at-once (all the power rules in one line) is a review landmark because nothing needs it on its own. It is also the skill exam papers test as 'the laws of indices'.
options: Review landmark (as drawn)
A topic, 'All the rules of powers together', needing negative powers and a power of a power
questions.lean: Landmark. A topic there would make fractional powers and the logarithm rules look as if they need negative powers, which they do not.

questions.q: The library loans quiz sits in Database Methods' Practice series, before 'A database with several tables', but it says it differs from 'a college timetable' and uses 'every table on the earlier pages in this module'. It is also the only page that teaches many-to-many links and a two-column key, and the map puts that topic after 'Designing a database'.
options: Move it to the end of 'A database with several tables', after a-college-timetable
Leave the course order and let the map show it after the timetable
questions.lean: Move it. The page itself assumes the timetable.
questions.answer: Move the quiz after the college timetable.

questions.q: 'Polynomials and like terms' now needs Python lists, as well as letters, powers and the order of operations, because both of its teaching pages keep a polynomial as a list from their first cell (collecting like terms is adding two lists place by place). That is true to the pages, but it puts the rest of algebra (expanding, factorising, graphs of functions, lines, the quadratic formula, limits and the derivative, depth 6 onwards) behind a first course in Python up to lists. A Zen learner who finishes 'Doing the same to both sides' has no next algebra town, and the derivative is now at depth 10.
options: Keep the need (as drawn): the map shows the pages as they are
Drop it, treating the list as the pages' notation, not the idea
Keep it, and plan a paper page on terms and like terms for the Zen module, which would take the need away
questions.lean: Keep it. A learner who has never met a list is lost in the first cell of both pages. If the Zen module grows past the balance, a paper page on terms and like terms is the page to write, and the need goes with it.
questions.answer: Keep the need, and plan a paper page on like terms for the Zen module.

notes:
REVISION. Revised from graph.json by the revise stage, in the light of three critics (size, needs, learner): 42 findings, 39 applied in whole or in part, 3 rejected. 185 topics (was 190), 41 districts (was 43), 11 regions, 32 landmarks; every page placed; maximum depth 12. Topics a finding created or reshaped carry "agreement": "critic".

Merged: list-comprehensions, python-grids and list-aliasing into list-comprehensions-and-grids ('List comprehensions, grids and copies': one 2,000-word page that later pages cite as one unit, cut into three towns of 340 to 1,200 words at depths 6 and 7); when-averages-mislead into mean-median-mode ('Averages, and which one to trust': nothing needed it, and both routes teach it before spread); bug-to-root-cause into debugging ('Finding a bug and its cause': the same idea on four courses' routes, and a teacher could not tell the two towns apart). Demoted to steps: normal-distribution (two optional 'go further' sections, now the last steps of spread-of-data) and matrices-in-numpy (the last step of inverse-matrices-and-systems; nothing needs it). New: testing-and-documenting-classes, from the object course's two pages that open on subclasses and so could not stay steps in topics that need no classes. Districts: averages-and-spread merged into data-and-charts ('Data, charts and averages'); matrix-methods and 3d-graphics merged into matrices-and-3d ('Matrices and 3D pictures'); git-and-github moved to Websites and browsers as 'Your tools: an editor and GitHub'; solving-equations-numerically moved from Algorithms to Calculus.

REGIONS. Number; Logic and binary; Algebra and graphs; Shape and space; Chance and data; Machine learning; Programming; Making software; Databases; Building web pages; Websites and browsers. How they came from the search areas: number split into Number (number basics, fractions, powers, roots and logarithms) and Logic and binary (numbers in a computer, sets and logic); its two Zen districts 'Lines, grids and graphs' and 'First equations' dissolved into algebra (coordinates and patterns-as-graphs into 'Grids and straight lines', log-scales into roots-and-logarithms, unknowns and balancing merged, below). Algebra-geometry split into Algebra and graphs (expressions, solving equations, quadratics, functions and their graphs, grids and straight lines, calculus) and Shape and space (measuring shapes, triangles and trigonometry with Pythagoras moved in, and, since the revision, one 'Matrices and 3D pictures' district). Chance-data split into Chance and data (five districts, four since the revision merged the two statistics districts; Markov chains moved into 'Simulations and models') and Machine learning (two districts: 'Machines that write', with two new topics for the text-generation pages, and 'Machines that learn'). Programming split into Programming (six districts; 'Searching and sorting' and 'Algorithms for hard problems' merged into 'Algorithms') and Making software (fixing mistakes, programs for people). The integrator's new 'Git and GitHub' district (the web area's editor, fork and Git history topics, programming's issues and pull requests, and a new GitHub account topic) sat in Making software; the revision moved it to Websites and browsers. Web split into Building web pages (HTML, CSS, layout, movement) and Websites and browsers (publishing and fixing a site, how a browser works, accessibility, a whole site); html-form-fields moved into HTML, sending-a-form into How a browser works, and the Full Stack topic page-reads-database into Databases' 'Data in and out'. Topic renames to avoid clashes: 'Matrices that move pictures' (the district was 'Matrices'), 'Fixing a broken web page' (the district is 'Finding and fixing mistakes'), 'Markov chains: where chances settle', 'Limits: what a function gets close to'.

NEIGHBOURS come from the needs that cross regions (counts after the revision): web pages-websites 17, programming-making software 12, algebra-shape and space 9, programming-chance and data 7, number-algebra 5, programming-machine learning 4, algebra-programming 3 (new: polynomials need lists, maths functions need Python functions, solving by computing needs binary search), programming-shape and space 3 (new: matrices need the comprehensions topic, perspective needs functions and loops), number-chance and data 3, logic and binary-programming 2, and the only link of each of these: logic and binary-number (binary needs powers), databases-web pages (the Full Stack page needs form fields). With the revised needs, its 2-opt pass, started from the file's region order, stops at a local best that puts logic and binary between websites and machine learning; restarts find 'number, algebra, shape and space, chance and data, programming, making software, machine learning, logic and binary, databases, web pages, websites' at a slightly lower cost. The next stage should look at the ring before trusting it.

MERGES (the same idea from two areas). algebraic-fractions: number and algebra both proposed it under that id; one topic in Fractions, needing adding and dividing fractions (the Zen page puts shapes in fractions itself, so it does not need letters). letters-for-numbers: number's unknown-numbers (Zen, a-box-with-something-in-it) and algebra's expressions-and-equations (Dewey and integrated sections): both teach that a letter stands for a number and an equation says two sides are equal. The integrator had it need order-of-operations; the revision moved that need to polynomials, because the Zen pages keep to one operation or a picture. balancing-equations: number's solving-by-balancing and algebra's balancing-equations were both built on keeping-it-level; one topic, 'Doing the same to both sides', replacing PRE-2. coordinates: number's topic is the site's one coordinates topic; every ext:coordinates resolves to it. PYTHON CLOSER LOOKS and other double placements. powers-in-python: only in first-lines-of-python (its misconception is ^ against **, met on first-steps), no longer in what-a-power-is. the-hidden-bracket: only in rearranging-formulas (it opens from rearranging-formulae), no longer in order-of-operations, whose plain text lost the fraction-bar sentence. equals-three-ways moved from python-variables to python-decisions: it opens from making-decisions and compares =, == and the maths =, so a learner needs == first. when-two-methods-agree (programming's elsewhere, suggested for chance-by-simulation) is a closer look in conditional-probability, because it opens from the Monty Hall page (three-doors), which is there; in chance-by-simulation it would refer to a page the learner has not reached. dividing-in-python, a-total-that-starts-again and when-is-a-breaks stay where programming put them; two-names-one-list is now in the merged list-comprehensions-and-grids. SIZE AND THE EFFORT TABLE, after the revision. The validator's median words per topic is about 1,050-1,600 at depths 0-4, 2,550 at depth 5, 3,190 at depth 6, about 2,100-2,200 at depths 7-9, and 4,200-4,500 at depths 10-11 (one or two topics each; the derivative and its rules, each with one page per course). Most of the high values are parallel routes added together. Taking the largest single-course route per topic instead, the median is about 950-1,500 words at depths 0-4 (Zen and web pages, small on purpose) and about 2,000-2,950 at depths 5-11: content roughly doubles with depth and stays within one to two sittings. The proxy splits a page evenly among the topics it teaches, so a topic that lists a shared page whole (mean-median-mode takes What is typical? apart from its spread sections) is undercounted. Heaviest single routes: css-3d (3,630 words at depth 5), inverse-matrices-and-systems (3,620 at depth 9, with the NumPy page), python-lists (3,620, A row of numbers), perspective-projection (3,550 at depth 5), venn-diagrams, matrices, linear-and-binary-search and function-scope (3,330 at depth 3 since python-functions stopped needing loops: one long Dewey page, one idea, 2.3 sittings; the Programming Foundations route is two sections). Lightest deep topics: could-it-be-luck (about 420 words at depth 8, a leaf, kept because it needs combinations, which simulation does not), solving-linear-equations and factorising-quadratics (about 800, where factorising by inspection is slow to learn), and the two planned towns. The validator's 'many pages teach it' warnings are for topics with one page, or a few sections of one page, per course (data-kinds-and-frequency, first-lines-of-python, spread-of-data with its two 'go further' steps, and debugging with four courses' routes).

QUESTIONS. The proposals' 26 questions became 15, and twelve after the revision. Settled by integration and dropped: where the text-generation pages go (algebra and chance both asked; they are in Machine learning); a Making software region (programming asked; yes); where the shared tools live (web asked; the integrator put Git and the editor in Making software, and the revision moved them to Websites and browsers, beside publishing and the inspector); the Zen graphs and equations districts (number asked; moved into algebra, and log scales kept with logarithms). Dropped as settled by the proposer's own lean with nothing new to add: review landmarks for the 'views from the top', 'How far to trust a simulation' as a topic, where 'Solving an equation by computing' lives (the revision moved it to Calculus), a database topic for set operations, and merging the form query with the Full Stack page. Merged into one gaps question: decimals, percentages and ratio; kinds of triangle; information theory; GROUP BY; HTML lists and tables; vectors; and, since the revision, multiplying negative numbers.

CONVENTIONS kept from the proposals: a step with section null means the page apart from any sections other topics list as their own teaching steps (an 'applies' or 'context' step elsewhere does not take a section away; logarithms' 'applies' step on how many bits is enough leaves that section in binary-numbers); a page split across topics lists each section where it teaches. A page can be both a landmark and a step (four-questions, a-program-of-your-own, building-it-together), and a page can be an 'applies' step for the whole and a teaching step for a named section in the same topic (the-tools-around-your-code in debugging).

tower.name: The Tower of Unknowing
tower.plain: Every traveller starts here, in the middle of Comath. Nobody in the tower knows anything yet, and that is the best place to begin.
tower.lore: Many leave the tower. Few explore all of Comath.

plains.name: The Prerequisite Plains
plains.plain: The towns around the tower. None of them needs anything first, so a traveller can start at any of them.
